newsitem.title: USA: US Sen urges Justice Dept to pursue yield burning.
newsitem.headline: US Sen urges Justice Dept to pursue yield burning.

text.p: U.S. Sen. Charles Grassley urged the U.S. Justice Department to investigate possible "yield burning" in the municipal bond market, to use the powerful False Claims Act to pursue Wall Street violators and to tell IRS to leave innocent localities alone.
Grassley made the remarks in a two-page letter to U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno.

The $1.3 trillion municipal bond market was stunned by recent charges that bond underwriters overbill issuers for U.S. Treasuries bought in the open market and used in bond financing transactions, a practiced dubbed yield burning.

The Internal Revenue Service notified issuers last year that they can avoid having interest on their bonds declared taxable by IRS if they pay Treasury the difference between the price they paid for securities and the spot price. Issuers uniformly opposed the plan.

"I strongly urge Justice Dept to investigate the circumstances on which the IRS action is based," Grassley said. "If the Department concludes that the overcharges occurred, then it should pursue all available remedies against any party which has violated the False Claims Act."

Under 1986 amendments to the federal false claims law, which Grassley sponsored, any entity that "knowingly submits or conspires to submit false claims for payment to the U.S. is liable for treble damanges and penalties," Grassley said.
"The False Claims Act may offer the Justice Department a powerful weapon," Grassley said.

"It appears that many of the nation's largest investment banking firms may have overcharged thousands of state and local agencies for securities they purchased in connection with municipal bond refundings. These overcharges were then unwittingly passed on to the Unites States by the local governments."

Grassley said it would be "devastating" to millions of bond holders if bonds were declared taxable. To avoid that, thousands of financially strapped hospitals, school districts and other bond issuers would have to step forward to make the payments, a "manifestly unfair" step, Grassley said.
